title: Master Ouyi on Faith, Vows, and Practice

inline.s: Question: Some articles say that Master Ouyi taught that so long as one has faith and vows, one is certain to attain rebirth. Others say that Master Ouyi taught that so long as one has true faith and earnest vows, even reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind will bring rebirth. Yet when I read Master Ouyi's Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra, I find quite the opposite — in the Yaojie, Master Ouyi teaches: faith gives rise to vows, and vows guide practice; practice fulfills the vows, and practice attests the faith. Of these three positions, which is correct?

Answer: Those who say "Master Ouyi taught that so long as one has faith and vows, one is certain to attain rebirth" base themselves on Master Ouyi's words: "Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the grade of one's birth depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding." They then interpret "whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows" as meaning: so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth. This interpretation is mistaken, for the following reasons:

First, if understood in this way, then "whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the grade of one's birth depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding" would mean: so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth; and so long as one has the practice of name-holding, one attains rebirth (with deep practice, one is reborn at a high grade; with shallow practice, at a low grade). In this way, the first half says that so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth, while the second half says that so long as one has the practice of name-holding, one attains rebirth. Then does rebirth depend on faith and vows alone, or on the practice of name-holding alone? Just think — how could Master Ouyi possibly have uttered such self-contradictory words?! Therefore one must pay particular attention to the difference in meaning between "quanyou" (entirely by virtue of) and "quanping" (entirely relying upon): "quanyou" expresses a necessary condition (an indispensable condition), while "quanping" expresses a sufficient condition (this condition alone being enough).

Second, the two sentences "whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the grade of one's birth depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding" come from Master Ouyi's Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra, which says: "Faith, vows, and name-holding — the essential purport of the whole sutra. Faith and vows are the wisdom-practice; name-holding is the practice-of-practice. Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the grade of one's birth depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding. Hence the wisdom-practice is the guide in front, and the practice-of-practice is the true cultivation — like the eyes and feet moving together."

The Annotated Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra

In this passage, "faith, vows, and name-holding — the essential purport of the whole sutra" means that faith, vows, and practice (name-holding) are inseparably linked; this is the essential purport of this sutra, and the essential path of Pure Land practice. "Faith and vows are the wisdom-practice; name-holding is the practice-of-practice," and "hence the wisdom-practice is the guide in front, and the practice-of-practice is the true cultivation, like the eyes and feet moving together" mean: faith and vows are the guide, like the eyes; name-holding is the true cultivation, like the two feet. Without eyes one walks blindly, and without feet one cannot move forward at all. Therefore, from the context of "whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the grade of one's birth depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding," the meaning of these two sentences is: one who attains rebirth must have faith and vows, and must also have the practice of name-holding — with deep practice, one is reborn at a high grade; with shallow practice, at a low grade.

In this passage, Master Ouyi states it very clearly: faith and vows are the guide in front (leading the way), and name-holding is the true cultivation (walking the road). How could it be acceptable to have only the guide without the true cultivation? Moreover, the master illustrates it vividly: faith and vows are like the eyes, name-holding is like the feet. If a traveler is to reach his destination (the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss), he must both look at the road with his eyes and walk with his feet (eyes and feet moving together). How could one reach the destination by merely having eyes to look at the road while the feet do not walk? Just as Master Ouyi teaches in the earlier section "Clarifying the Principle" of the Yaojie: "The principle is the essential path of practice... This sutra takes faith, vows, and name-holding as the essential principle of practice. Without faith, there is nothing to give rise to vows; without vows, there is nothing to guide practice; without the wondrous practice of name-holding, there is nothing to fulfill the vows and attest the faith... Faith means faith in oneself and faith in others, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in the principle and faith in the phenomena. Vows mean to detest and renounce Sahā and to yearn for Ultimate Bliss. Practice means to uphold the Name with one mind undisturbed." Please note that Master Ouyi says: "Practice means to uphold the Name with one mind undisturbed." Where does he ever say that practice is unnecessary, and that faith and vows alone will surely bring rebirth?

Those who say "Master Ouyi taught that so long as one has true faith and earnest vows, even reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind will surely bring rebirth" base themselves on Master Ouyi's words: "When faith is decisive and vows are earnest, even reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind will surely bring rebirth." (from the Discourse on Name-Holding Passing Through the Nine Grades and Purifying the Four Lands)

"When faith is decisive and vows are earnest, even reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind will surely bring rebirth" is an erroneous formulation. That is why Master Ouyi himself, in the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra, corrected this formulation and pointed out clearly: reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind does not necessarily bring rebirth; only when one recites to the point of one mind undisturbed is rebirth certain. The Yaojie says: "Question: Does reciting the name with a scattered mind also remove offenses? Answer: The merit of the name is inconceivable; how could it not remove offenses? But it does not necessarily bring rebirth, because leisurely, scattered good acts can hardly withstand the accumulated offenses of time without beginning. You should know that if our accumulated offenses had any form or substance, the whole of empty space could not contain them. Even if for a hundred years, day and night, one recited 'Amitābha' a hundred thousand times, each utterance extinguishing the birth-and-death of eight billion kalpas, still the offenses extinguished would be like soil on a fingernail, while the offenses not extinguished would be like the soil of the great earth. Only when one recites to the point of one mind undisturbed is one like a strong man breaking through a siege — no longer something the three armies can restrain."

Moreover, in the Yaojie Master Ouyi gives a comprehensive and profound exposition of the relationship among faith, vows, and practice: "Faith, vows, and name-holding — the essential purport of the whole sutra. Faith and vows are the wisdom-practice; name-holding is the practice-of-practice." And he says: "The wisdom-practice (faith and vows) is the guide in front, and the practice-of-practice (name-holding) is the true cultivation — like the eyes and feet moving together." Thus faith and vows are like the eyes, name-holding is like the feet; faith and vows are the guide in front, and name-holding is the true cultivation. Master Ouyi also gives a clear exposition of the content and requirements of faith, vows, and practice: "Faith means faith in oneself and faith in others, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in the principle and faith in the phenomena. Vows mean to detest and renounce Sahā and to yearn for Ultimate Bliss. Practice means to uphold the Name with one mind undisturbed." Thus the requirement of practice is: uphold the Name with one mind undisturbed. And Master Ouyi says: "Without faith, there is nothing to give rise to vows; without vows, there is nothing to guide practice; without the wondrous practice of name-holding (one mind undisturbed), there is nothing to fulfill the vows and attest the faith." Therefore, if one's faith is truly decisive and one's vows truly earnest, the result is bound to be one mind undisturbed. How could reciting with a scattered mind count as decisive faith and earnest vows? Is one to fulfill one's earnest vows by reciting with a scattered mind, and attest one's decisive faith by reciting with a scattered mind? Does this accord with the meaning of the sutra?

Concerning the relationship among true faith, earnest vows, and vigorous practice, Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, instructs: "Set aside the faithless for the moment (those without faith, put aside and speak not of them). As for the faithful — one who has faith but no vows is still as one without faith. One who has vows but no practice is still as one without vows. One whose practice is not vigorous is still as one without practice. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vows are not earnest; the reason the vows are not earnest is that the faith is not true. In a word, it is hard to give rise to true faith. If faith is truly genuine, the vows will of themselves become earnest. If the vows are truly earnest, the practice will of itself become vigorous. True and earnest faith and vows, joined to brave and vigorous practice, will decisively attain rebirth in the Pure Land, decisively behold Amitābha, decisively realize the three kinds of non-retrogression, and decisively become a Buddha in one more lifetime." (from the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)
From the above we may conclude: Master Ouyi's view of faith, vows, and practice is:
faith gives rise to vows, and vows guide practice; practice fulfills the vows, and practice attests the faith.

Master Yinguang greatly praised Master Ouyi, and especially Master Ouyi's Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra. Master Yinguang said: "The Amitābha Sūtra has the Essential Explanation written by Master Ouyi, which reaches the utmost in both principle and phenomena, the foremost commentary since the Buddha preached this sutra — most wondrous and most exact. Even if an ancient Buddha were to appear again in the world and re-comment on this sutra, he could not surpass it." (from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Letter to Ms. Xu Fuxian) And concerning whether reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind surely brings rebirth, Master Yinguang said: "Reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind can hardly attain rebirth." (from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou) From this we know that, on whether reciting with a scattered mind "also surely brings rebirth," one should take the view of the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra as the standard:
Reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind does not necessarily bring rebirth; only when one recites to the point of one mind undisturbed is rebirth certain.

Since even reciting with a scattered mind does not necessarily bring rebirth, then if one has faith and vows alone without actual practice, rebirth is even less certain. As for the claim that faith alone, without earnest vows and without vigorous practice, surely brings rebirth, that is still more groundless talk.
Question: Is it really so that even with true faith alone, or with true faith and earnest vows alone, rebirth is not certain? Please note: I am speaking of true faith and earnest vows.
Answer: With faith, one can give rise to vows; with vows, one can guide practice. Therefore, vows without vigorous practice
are not earnest vows
, and faith without earnest vows
is not true faith
. On this, Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, has spoken very clearly:
"The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vows are not earnest; the reason the vows are not earnest is that the faith is not true."

(The full text of this instruction: "Set aside the faithless for the moment (those without faith, put aside and speak not of them). As for the faithful — one who has faith but no vows is still as one without faith. One who has vows but no practice is still as one without vows. One whose practice is not vigorous is still as one without practice. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vows are not earnest; the reason the vows are not earnest is that the faith is not true. In a word, it is hard to give rise to true faith. If faith is truly genuine, the vows will of themselves become earnest. If the vows are truly earnest, the practice will of itself become vigorous. True and earnest faith and vows, joined to brave and vigorous practice, will decisively attain rebirth in the Pure Land, decisively behold Amitābha, decisively realize the three kinds of non-retrogression, and decisively become a Buddha in one more lifetime." (from the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)) Master Ouyi also states it very clearly in the Yaojie: "This sutra (the Amitābha Sūtra) takes faith, vows, and name-holding as the essential principle of practice. Without faith, there is nothing to give rise to vows; without vows, there is nothing to guide practice; without the wondrous practice of name-holding, there is nothing to fulfill the vows and attest the faith... Faith means faith in oneself and faith in others, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in the principle and faith in the phenomena. Vows mean to detest and renounce Sahā and to yearn for Ultimate Bliss. Practice means to uphold the Name with one mind undisturbed." Please note that Master Ouyi says: "Practice means to uphold the Name with one mind undisturbed."
